ECE 6390 / Navigation

Code-delay and Doppler search

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows why acquisition searches both code delay and carrier-frequency offset.

A delayed spreading code requires a matching local code phase. Carrier Doppler also rotates the received complex signal during integration. A correct code phase alone cannot make a frequency-mismatched signal add coherently.

For a constant residual frequency Δf over integration time T, normalized coherent power is |sinc(ΔfT)|², with sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx). The first frequency null is at |Δf| = 1/T. This example multiplies that factor by the squared periodic code correlation to form a separable teaching surface.

Longer integration makes the frequency peak narrower. A fixed frequency grid can miss a narrow between-bin peak, even in this noiseless model. Real acquisition also depends on the actual code ambiguity function, noise, data transitions, and detection thresholds; delay here is modulo a 31-chip teaching sequence.

Example

With T = 5 ms, the first coherent frequency null is 200 Hz from the true carrier offset. A 100 Hz mismatch gives |sinc(0.5)|² = 4/π² ≈ 0.405, approximately −3.92 dB power loss.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. If coherent integration time doubles, how should frequency-grid spacing change to preserve a similar worst-case coherent mismatch loss?

    Keep the maximum magnitude of ΔfT similar.

    Halve the frequency-grid spacing. The maximum between-bin mismatch then halves while T doubles, preserving their product.

    2. Why does a strong cyclic code-correlation peak still leave an absolute timing ambiguity?

    Consider delays separated by one complete code period.

    A repeated code gives the same cyclic alignment after each code period. The receiver needs additional epoch, navigation-message, or timing information to determine the absolute delay.
